item.title: Tropical Storm Isaias Public Advisory Number 5a
item.description:
Issued at 700 PM CDT Wed Oct 07 2026 
000
WTNT34 KNHC 072354
TCPAT4
 
BULLETIN
Tropical Storm Isaias Intermediate Advisory Number 5A
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL092026
700 PM CDT Wed Oct 07 2026
 
...AIR FORCE HURRICANE HUNTERS CURRENTLY INVESTIGATING ISAIAS...
...HURRICANE AND STORM SURGE WATCHES IN EFFECT FOR PORTIONS OF THE 
NORTHERN GULF COAST...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 700 PM CDT...0000 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...22.8N 92.4W
ABOUT 200 MI...325 KM WNW OF PROGRESO MEXICO
ABOUT 480 MI...775 KM SSW OF THE MOUTH OF THE MISSISSIPPI RIVER
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...65 MPH...100 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...ENE OR 65 DEGREES AT 8 MPH...13 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...994 MB...29.36 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
CHANGES WITH THIS ADVISORY:
 
None.
 
SUMMARY OF WATCHES AND WARNINGS IN EFFECT:
 
A Storm Surge Watch is in effect for...
* Mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown
 
A Hurricane Watch is in effect for...
* Bay St. Louis to Indian Pass
 
A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for...
* Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line to west of Bay St. Louis
* East of Indian Pass to Aucilla River
 
A Storm Surge Watch means there is a possibility of life- 
threatening inundation, from rising water moving inland from the 
coastline, in the indicated locations during the next 48 hours. For 
a depiction of areas at risk, please see the National Weather 
Service Storm Surge Watch/Warning Graphic, available at 
hurricanes.gov.
 
A Hurricane Watch means that hurricane conditions are possible 
within the watch area. A watch is typically issued 48 hours before 
the anticipated first occurrence of tropical-storm-force winds, 
conditions that make outside preparations difficult or dangerous.
 
A Tropical Storm Watch means that tropical storm conditions are
possible within the watch area, generally within 48 hours.
 
Interests in the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico and elsewhere
around the U.S. northern Gulf Coast should closely monitor the
progress of this system. Additional watches and warnings could be 
required for portions of the U.S. northern Gulf Coast tonight.
 
For storm information specific to your area, including possible
inland watches and warnings, please monitor products issued by your
local National Weather Service forecast office.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 700 PM CDT (0000 UTC), the center of Tropical Storm Isaias was 
located near latitude 22.8 North, longitude 92.4 West. Isaias is 
moving toward the east-northeast near 8 mph (13 km/h). A continued 
east-northeastward motion is expected tonight, followed by a turn 
toward the northeast and north on Thursday and Friday. On the 
forecast track, Isaias is expected to pass to the north of the 
Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday and make landfall along the U.S. 
northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 65 mph (100 km/h) with higher 
gusts. Isaias is forecast to become a hurricane by Thursday morning, 
with further strengthening expected through Friday morning. 
 
Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 60 miles (95 km)
from the center.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 994 mb (29.36 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
Key messages for Isaias can be found in the Tropical Cyclone
Discussion under AWIPS header MIATCDAT4 and WMO header WTNT44 KNHC.
 
STORM SURGE: The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the
tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded by
rising waters moving inland from the shoreline. The water could
reach the following heights above ground somewhere in the indicated
areas if the peak surge occurs at the time of high tide...
 
Ocean Springs, MS to Indian Pass, FL...5-7 ft
Mobile Bay...5-7 ft
Mouth of the Mississippi River, LA to Ocean Springs, MS...3-5 ft
Indian Pass, FL to Steinhatchee River, FL...4-6 ft
Steinhatchee River, FL to Yankeetown, FL...2-4 ft
Lake Pontchartrain...1-3 ft
 
The deepest water will occur along the immediate coast near and to 
the east of the landfall location, where the surge will be 
accompanied by large and dangerous waves. Surge-related flooding 
depends on the relative timing of the surge and the tidal cycle, and 
can vary greatly over short distances. For information specific to 
your area, please see products issued by your local National Weather 
Service forecast office.
 
For a complete depiction of areas at risk of storm surge inundation,
please see the National Weather Service Peak Storm Surge Graphic,
available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?peakSurge.
 
WIND: Hurricane conditions could begin in the Hurricane Watch area
late Friday, and tropical storm conditions could begin in the
watch areas by midday Friday.
 
Gusty winds are possible in portions of the Yucatan Peninsula on 
Thursday.
 
RAINFALL: Isaias is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 1 to 3
inches through Thursday across coastal portions of the eastern Bay
of Campeche with isolated higher amounts possible in the states of
Campeche and western Yucatan.
 
From Friday through the weekend, the system is expected to produce
rainfall amounts of 3 to 7 inches, with localized totals up to 10
inches, across the central U.S. Gulf Coast extending from far
southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Rainfall amounts of
1 to 3 inches, with localized amounts up to 5 inches, are possible
across much of the Southeast as far north as the Tennessee Valley
and the Carolinas. Flash and urban flooding, along with isolated
river flooding, will be possible.
 
For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with 
Isaias, please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall 
Graphic available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?rainqpf and 
the Flash Flood Risk graphic at 
hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ero
 
TORNADOES: Tornado potential will increase as rain bands 
accompanying Isaias approach the northeastern Gulf Coast Friday 
evening and overnight. This potential will spread inland on Saturday 
as Isaias continues northward.
 
SURF: Swells will affect the western and northern portions of the 
Yucatan Peninsula beginning on Thursday and spread northward toward 
the Gulf Coast late this week. These swells are likely to cause 
life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult 
products from your local weather office.
 
A depiction of rip current risk for the United States can be found
at: hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ripCurrents
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 1000 PM CDT.
 
$$
Forecaster Reinhart

item.title: Tropical Storm Isaias Forecast Discussion Number 5
item.description:
Issued at 400 PM CDT Wed Oct 07 2026 
592 
WTNT44 KNHC 072049
TCDAT4
 
Tropical Storm Isaias Discussion Number   5
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL092026
400 PM CDT Wed Oct 07 2026
 
Satellite and aircraft data show that Isaias continues to 
strengthen.  GOES-19 imagery indicates that a central dense overcast 
has formed, and the system has become more symmetric than this 
morning.  The peak NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft 700-mb winds 
were 61 kt, with the pressure dropping to 994 mb.  The initial 
intensity is set to 55 kt as a reflection of this data.
 
Isaias is basically on track, moving east-northeast at 7 kt. There 
is no change to the synoptic reasoning as a deepening trough along 
the northwestern Gulf Coast and a strengthening Atlantic subtropical 
ridge should cause the system to move faster to the northeast 
tomorrow and northward on Friday.  As long as the cyclone remains 
intact, it makes physical sense that the system will move on the 
faster and eastward side of the guidance due to the stronger shear 
Isaias should encounter near landfall.  Thus, the new forecast is 
adjusted slightly to the east, closer to the AI-based and 
corrected-consensus models.
 
NOAA radar data (P3-TDR) show that the system is experiencing some 
southwesterly shear, with tilt analyses displaying the mid-level 
circulation displaced 5-10 n mi to the northeast of the low-level 
center.  This structure seems sufficient for further intensification 
given a continuation of similar low or moderate shear and very warm 
SSTs in a very humid environment.  Models are fairly consistent 
about the shear increasing on Friday, but almost all guidance still 
shows a category 1 or 2 hurricane at landfall.  While the regional 
hurricane models have generally come down on the peak intensity this 
cycle, it is unknown whether this is the start of a real trend, and 
we would prefer to see more than one guidance cycle before making 
any adjustments.  The new forecast is close to the previous one, 
near the high side of the model suite.
 
Key Messages:
 
1. Isaias is expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when 
it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday. There is an 
increasing risk of life-threatening storm surge along portions of 
the northern Gulf Coast, and a Storm Surge Watch is in effect from 
The Mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida. Residents 
in the watch area should follow advice given by local officials and 
evacuate if told to do so.

2. The risk of damaging hurricane-force winds is increasing over 
portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, and southern 
Mississippi.  A Hurricane Watch has been issued from Bay St. Louis, 
Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida.  Residents in these areas 
should prepare for the possibility of long-duration power outages. 

3. Isaias will bring areas of heavy rainfall to the central U.S. 
Gulf Coast and much of the Southeast Friday into the weekend. Flash 
and urban flooding, along with isolated river flooding, will be 
possible.

4. Isaias could bring gusty winds and areas of heavy rain to the 
western portion of the Yucatan Peninsula through Thursday.
